summary: Bright Smiles Family Dentistry: 32 of 63 checks found a problem (19 specific to dental practices, 24 measured, 8 editorial). 3 urgent. Start with: Click-to-call phone number; Health information in forms next to tracking pixels; Patient form submits insecurely. 8 items need the owner to confirm a fact. 8 checks did not run (see limitations). No overall score is assigned.

topFindings.title: Click-to-call phone number
topFindings.why: Most dental appointments still start with a phone call, usually from a phone. Without a tappable number, a patient has to memorize or copy it.

topFindings.title: Health information in forms next to tracking pixels
topFindings.why: A dental practice is a HIPAA covered entity. Meta, TikTok and Google Ads pixels on a page where patients type “tooth pain, Delta Dental, DOB” have been the basis of class actions and OCR enforcement since the 2022 HHS tracking bulletin. This is a legal exposure, not a UX nit.

topFindings.title: Patient form submits insecurely
topFindings.why: A form that emails or GETs health details sends them in plain text through systems no BAA covers. Patients cannot see this; regulators can.

topFindings.title: Appointment booking route
topFindings.why: Roughly half of prospective patients prefer to book outside office hours. Phone-only booking loses them to a practice with online scheduling.

topFindings.title: New-patient path
topFindings.why: A first-time patient is deciding whether this office is easy to deal with. “Are you taking new patients, what do I fill out, what do I bring, how long will it take” are the four questions they arrive with.

findings.title: Click-to-call phone number

evidence.detail: No tel: link on any of 5 fetched pages. A phone number written as plain text cannot be tapped on a phone.

findings.impact: Most dental appointments still start with a phone call, usually from a phone. Without a tappable number, a patient has to memorize or copy it.
findings.fix: Wrap the office number in an <a href="tel:+1…"> link in the site header and footer, and on the contact and emergency pages.

findings.title: Health information in forms next to tracking pixels

evidence.method: Static HTML: form fields and third-party script hosts
evidence.detail: Form fields that would carry health or insurance details: Date of Birth, Insurance Provider, Reason for Visit / Describe your dental concern, Are you a new patient?. Advertising trackers on the same page: connect.facebook.net. Analytics/session tools: www.googletagmanager.com, static.hotjar.com.

findings.impact: A dental practice is a HIPAA covered entity. Meta, TikTok and Google Ads pixels on a page where patients type “tooth pain, Delta Dental, DOB” have been the basis of class actions and OCR enforcement since the 2022 HHS tracking bulletin. This is a legal exposure, not a UX nit.
findings.fix: Remove advertising pixels from every page with a form (or from the whole site), or move intake to a HIPAA-compliant forms vendor with a signed BAA. Review the tag manager container; use server-side conversion tracking without PHI if ads must be measured.
findings.rationale: Based on the HHS OCR bulletin on online tracking technologies (Dec 2022, updated Mar 2024). Parts were vacated for unauthenticated pages in June 2024, but a form that asks for symptoms or insurance is exactly the case the bulletin still covers.

findings.title: Patient form submits insecurely

evidence.detail: posts by mailto: (mailto:frontdesk@brightsmiles.example)

findings.impact: A form that emails or GETs health details sends them in plain text through systems no BAA covers. Patients cannot see this; regulators can.
findings.fix: Submit forms over HTTPS with POST to a HIPAA-compliant handler or forms vendor; never use mailto: for anything beyond a name and phone number.

findings.title: Appointment booking route

evidence.detail: No booking link, scheduling widget or appointment form on 5 fetched pages.

findings.impact: Roughly half of prospective patients prefer to book outside office hours. Phone-only booking loses them to a practice with online scheduling.
findings.fix: Add real-time online scheduling from your practice management system or a vendor (NexHealth, LocalMed, Flex, Zocdoc, etc.), or at minimum a short appointment-request form with a stated callback time.

findings.title: New-patient path

evidence.detail: No new-patient or first-visit page among 5 fetched pages.

findings.impact: A first-time patient is deciding whether this office is easy to deal with. “Are you taking new patients, what do I fill out, what do I bring, how long will it take” are the four questions they arrive with.
findings.fix: Create a /new-patients page: accepting-new-patients statement, how to book, what the first visit includes and how long it takes, what to bring, insurance and payment basics, and a link to forms.
findings.effort: 3–5 hours: owner input plus one page

findings.title: Insurance and payment clarity

evidence.detail: No insurer is named. No in-network / participating-provider statement. Vague wording: “…ral health and exceptional dental care. We accept all insurance plans. Call us today! Learn More Read M…”. No financing provider named. No in-house membership plan mentioned.

findings.impact: “We accept most insurance” is the sentence patients trust least. They want to know whether you are in network with their plan, because that decides their bill.
findings.fix: Publish an insurance page that lists the plans you are in network with, explains how out-of-network billing works, names your financing partner and any in-house membership plan, and says what an uninsured new-patient visit costs.
findings.effort: 2–3 hours: owner provides the list; one page

findings.title: Emergency and after-hours instructions

evidence.detail: No emergency or urgent-care wording on 5 fetched pages.

findings.impact: Someone searching “emergency dentist near me” at 9 pm is in pain and will call the first office whose site tells them what to do. This is the highest-intent traffic a practice gets.
findings.fix: Create an /emergency page with: the number to call, what happens after hours (answering service, on-call dentist, or “go to the ER if…”), which problems are true emergencies, and whether same-day visits are realistic.
findings.effort: 2–3 hours: owner decides routing; one page

findings.title: Service pages that lead to a next step

evidence.detail: 0 individual service pages fetched; sitemap suggests about 1 service URLs in total. Sedation/anxiety options are mentioned. Children/family wording is present.

findings.impact: Patients search for the procedure (“dental implants near me”), not the practice. One page listing twenty services cannot rank for any of them or answer the question “should I come to you for this?”.
findings.fix: Create one page per high-value service (implants, Invisalign, emergency, crowns, whitening, kids): who it is for, what the visit involves, how long, cost range or how it is estimated, and a book/call action.
findings.effort: 4–8 hours per page for the top five services

findings.title: Privacy policy and HIPAA notice

evidence.detail: No privacy, HIPAA or notice-of-privacy link on 5 fetched pages.

findings.impact: Any site with a form needs a privacy policy, and a dental practice must post its HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices. Its absence is the first thing a complaint investigator checks.
findings.fix: Add a footer link to a privacy policy that covers the forms and trackers in use, and a link to the Notice of Privacy Practices.

findings.title: Advertising claims a dental board may question

evidence.detail: “no further for all of your dental needs. We offer painless dentistry and we guarantee you will love your new” — promises an outcome (“painless”) no clinician can guarantee.
“dental needs. We offer painless dentistry and we guarantee you will love your new smile. Dr. Smith is a cosm” — offers a guarantee; many boards treat guaranteed results as misleading.
“stry and family dentistry. We have been voted the best dentist in Fairview and we are the #1 choice for families” — superiority claim that must be substantiated and attributed (who voted, when).

“fect. I used to hate the dentist!” — Jennifer R. “Best dental office in Fairview. The whole staff is wonderful.” — Mar” — superiority claim that must be substantiated and attributed (who voted, when).
“Veneers, teeth whitening and smile makeovers. We guarantee results you will love and our whitening is perman” — offers a guarantee; many boards treat guaranteed results as misleading.

findings.impact: State dental practice acts prohibit false, misleading or unverifiable advertising, and competitors do file complaints. “Painless”, “guaranteed” and “best” are the usual triggers.
findings.fix: Rewrite to what you can substantiate: “we use topical and local anesthetic and go slowly”, “voted Best of [City] 2025 by [publication]”, “most whitening lasts 1–3 years with touch-ups”.
findings.rationale: The text is objectively present; whether a given state board would act on it is a judgement, so confidence is medium. Have the dentist review against their state’s rules.

findings.title: “Specialist” wording for a non-recognised specialty

evidence.detail: “…d we guarantee you will love your new smile. Dr. Smith is a cosmetic dentistry specialist and specializes in implant dentistry, sedation dentistry an…”
“…new smile. Dr. Smith is a cosmetic dentistry specialist and specializes in implant dentistry, sedation dentistry and family dentistry. We have…”
“…dental technology in a relaxing environment. Dr. Smith is a cosmetic dentistry specialist who is passionate about creating beautiful smiles. Our frie…”

findings.impact: Cosmetic, implant, sedation and family dentistry are not ADA-recognised specialties. Many states let only licensed specialists use “specialist”/“specializes in”; a general dentist can be disciplined for it.
findings.fix: Use “focuses on”, “with advanced training in” or “provides” instead, and name the actual training (e.g. “AAID credentialed”, “300+ hours of implant CE”).
findings.rationale: Rules differ by state and courts have struck some down on First Amendment grounds; this is a review flag for the dentist, not a verdict.

findings.title: Image alternative text

evidence.detail: 1 of 3 images lack an alt attribute. Empty alt can be appropriate for decoration; meaning is not certified.

findings.impact: People using screen readers may miss information carried by meaningful images.
findings.fix: Add useful alt text to informative images; use empty alt for purely decorative images after a visual review.
findings.effort: 1–3 hours: image purpose and text review

findings.title: Patient testimonials and before/after photos need authorization

evidence.detail: Named patient testimonials quoted on the site.
Before/after or smile gallery content. No “results may vary / actual patient” disclaimer found.

findings.impact: Using a patient’s name, photo or treatment story in marketing requires a signed HIPAA marketing authorization, separate from the consent to treat. Several states also require a disclaimer on before/after images.
findings.fix: Keep a signed authorization on file for every named testimonial and photo; add “Actual patient. Individual results vary.” under galleries; remove anything you cannot document.

findings.title: The dentist is a real, identifiable person

evidence.detail: A “Dr. …” is mentioned but no DDS/DMD credential appears beside the name. Biography page: https://brightsmiles.example/ covers a portrait.

findings.impact: People choose a dentist, not a building. A nervous patient wants to see who will be in their mouth, where they trained and how long they have practised; a faceless site reads like a corporate chain.
findings.fix: Add a Meet-the-Dentist page per clinician: real portrait, name with DDS/DMD, dental school, year started, memberships, one paragraph on how they treat anxious patients, and a booking link.
findings.effort: 2–4 hours per dentist, plus a photo session

findings.title: Address, map and getting there

evidence.detail: Visible street address matching structured data on 1 pages. No Google Maps directions link. Parking is not mentioned.

findings.impact: A local business that hides its address looks temporary. Patients also want to know about parking before they commit to a 7:30 am appointment.
findings.fix: Show the full address in the footer, mark it up in Dentist schema, and add a “Get directions” link to the exact Google Maps listing plus a sentence about parking and the entrance.

findings.title: Dentist structured data for local search

evidence.detail: "LocalBusiness" node: telephone, address, url present; missing geo, hours, image; type is not Dentist/DentalClinic.

findings.impact: The practice node exists; the gaps limit how confidently Google ties the site to the listing and shows hours and location.
findings.fix: Complete the node: geo, hours, image, use @type Dentist.

findings.title: Self-serving review markup

evidence.detail: "LocalBusiness" node carries aggregateRating.

findings.impact: Google stopped showing star snippets for reviews a business publishes about itself in 2019. This markup is ignored at best and treated as spammy at worst; many dental templates still ship it.
findings.fix: Remove aggregateRating/review from the Dentist/LocalBusiness node. Earn stars through the Google Business Profile instead.

findings.title: Heading structure

evidence.detail: Heading levels: H1 Welcome to Our Practice | H1 Bright Smiles Family Dentistry | H2 Our Services | H2 What Our Patients Say. More than one H1 is a review signal, not automatically an accessibility failure.

Heading levels: H1 Our Services | H3 General Dentistry | H3 Cosmetic Dentistry | H3 Restorative Dentistry | H3 Periodontal Therapy | H3 Pediatric Dentistry | H3 Sedation Dentistry | H2 Before and After Gallery. More than one H1 is a review signal, not automatically an accessibility failure.

findings.impact: An unclear heading outline makes key information harder to scan and navigate.
findings.fix: Use a clear primary page heading and logical subsections; confirm the rendered accessibility tree.

findings.impact: Screen readers pick a voice from the lang attribute; without it, English copy can be read with the wrong pronunciation rules. It is also a WCAG requirement.
findings.fix: Add lang="en" (or the page language) to the <html> element in the template.

findings.title: Footer copyright year

evidence.detail: Footer copyright year(s): 2021; current year 2026.

findings.impact: A footer that says © two years ago is the quickest way to make a visitor wonder whether the office is still open. It is also the most common defect on dental websites.
findings.fix: Output the year dynamically in the footer template.

findings.title: Homepage title names the city

evidence.detail: Title: “Bright Smiles Family Dentistry”; visible locality: Suite 210.

findings.impact: People search “dentist in [city]”. A title tag that is just the practice name wastes the strongest local relevance signal the page has.
findings.fix: Use a title like “[Practice] | Dentist in Suite 210” on the homepage, and “[Service] in Suite 210 | [Practice]” on service pages.

findings.title: Dated content that has gone quiet

evidence.detail: Most recent dated item: 2022-03-14 (about 55 months ago).

findings.impact: A blog whose last post is years old makes a visitor wonder whether the practice is still open. It is better to have no dates than old ones.
findings.fix: Either commit to one useful post a quarter (new-patient FAQs, insurance changes, a new hygienist) or remove the dates and the “blog” label.
findings.effort: 30 minutes to remove dates; ongoing otherwise

findings.title: Patient forms are PDF only

evidence.detail: PDF form links: https://brightsmiles.example/forms/new-patient-registration.pdf, https://brightsmiles.example/forms/medical-history.pdf; no online intake vendor link observed.

findings.impact: Printable PDFs assume a printer and a scanner. Many patients will skip them and the front desk ends up re-keying paper, or asking people to arrive 20 minutes early.
findings.fix: Move intake to a HIPAA-compliant digital forms tool (most practice management systems offer one) and keep the PDF as a fallback.
findings.rationale: Opinion based on front-desk workflow, not a measured defect: PDF forms work, they just push work onto the patient and the staff.

findings.title: Nothing for patients without insurance

evidence.detail: Insurance text exists but no financing partner, in-house membership plan or self-pay guidance was found.

findings.impact: About a third of US adults have no dental coverage. If the site only talks about insurance, those visitors assume they cannot afford you.
findings.fix: Add a short “No insurance?” section: an in-house membership plan if you have one, your financing partner, and the price of a new-patient exam and x-rays.
findings.rationale: Opinion: a practice may deliberately focus on insured patients; this is a missed-opportunity flag, not a defect.

findings.title: Copy that could be any dental office

evidence.detail: Stock phrases on the homepage: “state-of-the-art”, “caring team”, “comprehensive dental care”, “smile of your dreams”, “treat you like family”, “committed to excellence”, “highest quality”, “comfortable environment”, “latest technology”, “personalized treatment”, “your dental home”, “dental needs”, “all of your dental needs”, “look no further”, “we are dedicated to”, “passionate about”, “optimal oral health”, “exceptional dental care”.

findings.impact: These phrases appear on most dental websites in any city. A patient comparing three practices in three tabs cannot tell them apart, so they pick on price or proximity.
findings.fix: Replace each stock phrase with a specific, checkable fact: how long the first visit is, how you handle anxious patients, what the hygienist does differently, a real photo of the room.
findings.rationale: Phrase matching cannot judge tone; it only shows the copy is indistinguishable from the template default. Four or more matches on one page is a strong signal, two is a hint.

findings.title: Clinical vocabulary patients do not use

evidence.detail: 10 clinical terms across 1 sampled pages: restorative dentistry → fillings, crowns and repairs; periodontal → gum disease / gum treatment; endodontic → root canal; prosthodontics → crowns, bridges and dentures; composite resin → tooth-coloured filling; caries → cavities; malocclusion → crooked teeth or a bad bite; bruxism → teeth grinding.

findings.impact: Patients search for “deep cleaning” and “root canal”, not “scaling and root planing” or “endodontic therapy”. Jargon reads as the practice talking to itself, and it does not match search queries.
findings.fix: Use the patient’s word first and the clinical term in brackets once: “deep cleaning (scaling and root planing)”. Keep the clinical term for the service page title only if patients actually search it.
findings.rationale: Some of these terms are fine on a detailed service page for an informed patient; the flag is about density on the pages a new patient reads first.

findings.title: The homepage headline says who, what and where

evidence.detail: H1: “Welcome to Our Practice”. Mentions what you do: false; mentions where: false.

findings.impact: “Welcome to our practice” tells a visitor nothing they did not know from the URL. The headline is the one sentence everyone reads; it should answer “am I in the right place?” in a glance.
findings.fix: Try a headline shaped like “[Specific promise] dentistry in Suite 210” or “The dentist Suite 210 families see for [service]”, with the practice name in the logo rather than the H1.
findings.rationale: Headline quality is a judgement; the objective part is only whether the H1 names a place and a service. Treat the suggestion as a starting point.

findings.title: Stock photos where patients expect real people

evidence.detail: 3 images whose filenames or hosts identify a stock library, e.g. /images/shutterstock_1092384756.jpg, /images/istock-9981234-happy-family.jpg, /images/AdobeStock_334455667.jpeg.

findings.impact: Patients recognise the smiling stock family instantly, and it signals the practice could not be bothered to show its own team or rooms. Real photos are the cheapest trust signal a dental site can add.
findings.fix: Replace hero and team images with photos of the actual dentist, staff, reception and operatories (two hours with a local photographer). Keep stock only for abstract illustrations.
findings.effort: Half a day including a photo session
findings.rationale: The filenames prove the source; whether a given photo hurts is a judgement. Stock is more damaging on the homepage and team page than on a blog post.

findings.title: Copy talks about the practice more than the patient

evidence.detail: Homepage uses we/our/us 17 times and you/your 7 times (71% practice-focused).

findings.impact: The page is a description of the practice. Patients read looking for themselves: will I be in pain, what will it cost, how long will it take, can I come on Saturday.
findings.fix: Rewrite the hero and the first two sections from the patient’s side: “Your first visit takes about an hour” instead of “We offer comprehensive new-patient exams”.
findings.rationale: A pronoun ratio is a crude proxy for perspective; it is reliable at the extremes and noisy in the middle, hence medium confidence and a 65% threshold.

findings.title: One obvious thing to do next

evidence.detail: 1 distinct action labels on the homepage: “contact us”.

findings.impact: A visitor who is ready should see one clear action: call or book. “Learn more” buttons everywhere make them hunt.
findings.fix: Use two primary actions (“Call (555) 123-4567” and “Book online”) in the header and after each section; demote everything else to text links.
findings.rationale: Counting labels cannot see visual hierarchy; a page with eight links can still have one obvious button. Check the rendered page before acting.

findings.title: Office hours where patients look

evidence.detail: Hours wording “…10, Fairview, TX 75000 Hours: Monday - Thursday 8:00am - 5:00pm New patient forms: Download R…” on 1 pages; not on the homepage or footer.

findings.impact: Hours are the second thing people check after the phone number, often from the car. If they are only on the contact page, half the visitors never see them.
findings.fix: Put the weekly hours in the footer template and keep them identical to the Google listing.

findings.title: Reading level of the copy

evidence.method: Readability formula on paragraph and list text
evidence.detail: Flesch–Kincaid grade 10.6 over 220 words of paragraph text.

findings.impact: The copy averages grade 10.6 (worst: 10.6 on https://brightsmiles.example/). Patients skim dental sites on a phone in a waiting room or in pain; copy that reads like a journal article gets skipped.
findings.fix: Aim for grade 6–8: shorter sentences, one idea each, everyday words, and explain any clinical term the first time it appears.
findings.effort: 2–4 hours of editing for the main pages
findings.rationale: Flesch–Kincaid is a blunt instrument (it penalises long but familiar words like “appointment”), so this is a prompt to read the page aloud, not a hard rule.

findings.title: Call and book buttons visible on a phone without scrolling
findings.impact: This requires a rendered browser check.
findings.fix: Browser inspection disabled by configuration.

findings.title: Complete scheduling and form interaction
findings.impact: Reachable pages do not prove that a patient can complete the booking or receive confirmation.
findings.fix: Manually verify mobile menus, conditional forms, validation messages, correct office selection, scheduling slot selection, and booking confirmation in a provider-approved test environment. No live forms, calls or appointments are submitted by this tool.

findings.title: Owner-authorized profile and performance checks
findings.impact: An owner connection can expose supported profile details and performance windows beyond public sources.
findings.fix: Obtain owner consent and use a Google Cloud project approved for the Business Profile APIs; Places access does not authorize Business Profile management. Configure a Google OAuth consent screen and OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow with business.manage. Select the owner-managed account and exact location ID, then verify it against the website. Add a read-only provider implementing this report contract: Business Information for location facts/categories/hours, supported Place Actions for appointment links, and supported reviews/media endpoints for reviews, owner replies and photos. Do not expose write actions in this audit. Use the Business Profile Performance API only with owner authorization and approved access. Report the supported metrics/date windows; unavailable metrics stay not tested. No private performance data is accessed in V0. Store tokens encrypted on the server with revocation, least privilege, retention/deletion controls and an OAuth 2.1 MCP authorization layer for the linked plugin account. This V0 intentionally has no token connection endpoint.
findings.effort: Separate integration: approved Google API project, OAuth review, account/location selection and security work

findings.title: Reviews patients can verify

evidence.detail: Review widget vendor detected (static.elfsight.com). No link to Google, Yelp or Healthgrades reviews.

findings.impact: Patients read Google reviews before they read your website. Hand-picked quotes on your own site carry little weight; a live feed or a link to the real profile does.
findings.fix: Keep responding to reviews; the responses are read as much as the reviews.

findings.title: Page status codes

evidence.detail: HTTP 200.

findings.impact: A failed public page prevents visitors and crawlers from reaching its content.
findings.fix: Repair or redirect the failing page to a relevant destination; update incoming links.

findings.title: HTTPS on fetched pages

evidence.detail: Final page URL: https://brightsmiles.example/. Certificate verification is enabled on HTTPS requests.

findings.impact: An unencrypted page undermines trust and can expose data entered on the website.
findings.fix: Enable a valid HTTPS certificate and redirect HTTP to HTTPS before offering forms.

findings.title: Insecure resource references

evidence.detail: 0 HTTP resource references: . Browser blocking depends on resource type.

findings.impact: Mixed resources can be blocked or loaded insecurely, affecting appearance and trust.
findings.fix: Serve referenced images, scripts, styles and frames over HTTPS; retest the rendered pages.

findings.title: Canonical URLs

evidence.detail: Canonical: https://brightsmiles.example/.

findings.impact: Canonical hints can be ambiguous or invalid, especially with duplicate URL variants.
findings.fix: Set valid canonical URLs reflecting the intended indexable page, then verify redirects and sitemap URLs.

findings.title: HTML indexability signals

evidence.detail: Robots/X-Robots-Tag: (none observed). This checks directives, not actual Google indexing.

findings.impact: A noindex directive can prevent an important public page from appearing in search.
findings.fix: Confirm the page should be public; remove unintended noindex directives and verify using owner-authorized Search Console.

findings.title: robots.txt crawl policy

evidence.detail:
HTTP 200; User-agent: *
Allow: /
Sitemap: https://brightsmiles.example/sitemap.xml; homepage crawl allowed: true.

findings.impact: Crawl permissions affect what this tool and compliant crawlers can inspect.
findings.fix: Review intended public crawl permissions; no robots file is required for an unrestricted public site.

findings.title: Sitemap discovery

evidence.detail: HTTP 200; 5 URL or child-sitemap entries found. Child sitemap recursion is outside V0.

findings.impact: A usable sitemap helps crawlers discover the intended pages but does not guarantee indexing.
findings.fix: Confirm the canonical sitemap is advertised in robots.txt and contains public canonical URLs. A sitemap at another path may already exist.

findings.title: Bounded broken-link check

evidence.detail: 2 additional unique internal/booking links checked; 0 could not be completed. Fetched page status codes are checked separately.

findings.impact: Broken links interrupt service research and contact journeys.
findings.fix: Replace broken destinations with useful equivalent pages; manually check any destinations that blocked requests.

findings.title: Form labels

evidence.detail: 0 fields lack an associated visible or ARIA label in static HTML. Dynamic form labels are checked in the browser.

findings.impact: Unlabeled controls are harder to use with assistive technology and can increase form errors.
findings.fix: Associate every input with an accessible label and specific error/help text; verify keyboard operation.

findings.title: Script and render-blocking review

evidence.detail: 4 external scripts, 4 potentially blocking stylesheet/script references, 1 font link/preload references. These counts do not establish whether a script is unnecessary.

findings.impact: Large dependency chains can delay useful content, particularly on mobile networks.
findings.fix: Use the performance trace and a tag inventory to establish owners and necessity; defer nonessential scripts and load critical styles/fonts efficiently.

findings.title: Mobile viewport declaration

evidence.detail: meta viewport: width=device-width,initial-scale=1.

findings.impact: Without a viewport meta tag, phones render the desktop layout shrunk to fit; text becomes unreadable and buttons untappable. Most dental traffic is mobile.
findings.fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the document head template.

findings.title: Third-party services loaded by the site

evidence.detail: 6 external hosts: connect.facebook.net (4 pages), www.googletagmanager.com (2 pages), cdn.callrail.com (1 page), static.elfsight.com (1 page), fonts.googleapis.com (1 page), static.hotjar.com (1 page).

findings.impact: An inventory for the developer: every external host is a performance cost, a privacy question and a thing that can break. Dental sites accumulate chat widgets, review feeds and pixels from successive agencies.
findings.fix: Confirm each vendor is still paid for and wanted; remove the rest. Check the privacy section for pixels on form pages.

rewrites.reason: Most dental appointments still start with a phone call, usually from a phone. Without a tappable number, a patient has to memorize or copy it. Roughly half of prospective patients prefer to book outside office hours. Phone-only booking loses them to a practice with online scheduling. A local business that hides its address looks temporary. Patients also want to know about parking before they commit to a 7:30 am appointment. A consistent name, address, phone, hours and useful landing page let patients recognize the same office across the website and Maps. Hours are the second thing people check after the phone number, often from the car. If they are only on the contact page, half the visitors never see them.
